bibliographic.title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence Into a Medical Curriculum: Evolving Student Perceptions and Faculty Development Challenges
bibliographic.authors: Kinner L. Flaglor, Gabrielle Rueff, Paul Monaco, Antonio E. Rusinol, Mark Hernandez
bibliographic.citation_apa: Flaglor, K. L., Rueff, G., Monaco, P., Rusinol, A. E., & Hernandez, M. (2026). Integration of artificial intelligence into a medical curriculum: Evolving student perceptions and faculty development challenges. Cureus. https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.109621

methodology.method_family: longitudinal survey comparison and faculty workshop evaluation
methodology.study_design: Repeated cohort surveys (2024 vs 2025 incoming M1; January 2025 vs January 2026 rising M3) plus pre-post faculty development workshops
methodology.sample_description: Medical students and faculty at East Tennessee State University Quillen College of Medicine; rising third-year students (class size 80); workshop participants
methodology.sample_size: Rising M3: n=62 (2025), n=68 (2026); Workshop 1: N=25 pre, 15 post; Workshop 2: N=16 pre, 7 post
methodology.technology_context: Generative AI and LLMs in medical curriculum; tools named include ChatGPT and Claude; faculty workshops on AI teaching integration, ethics, and policy

eligibility.decision_rationale: The study addresses generative AI and LLMs in a regulated healthcare education setting and proposes a multi-dimensional framework for responsible AI integration with ethical and policy-focused faculty development. However, the provided text does not address conversational AI system governance such as chatbots, agents, guardrails, observability, audit logs, tracing, handoff, or post-deployment operational controls.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Python triage marked central_candidate, but extracted text centers on curriculum integration, student perceptions, and faculty workshops rather than conversational governance in deployed LLM systems.

appraisal.notes: Single-institution medical education study using a previously published satisfaction instrument and pre-post workshop measures; statistical comparisons reported with means, SD, t-statistics, and p-values. Limitations section referenced in evidence hits but full limitations text not provided.

cerqual.explanation: Findings are internally coherent and tied to survey and workshop data, but relevance to conversational governance in regulated LLM systems is indirect; the study focuses on educational integration and faculty readiness rather than governance of conversational AI deployments.

coding.theme: Responsible generative AI integration in medical education
coding.subtheme: Faculty development and evolving student perceptions

synthesis.main_claim: Integrating generative AI into medical education requires sustained faculty development and mission-aligned training; student AI use and attitudes are shifting, while faculty workshops increased confidence and practical engagement but also produced more cautious ethical awareness.
synthesis.contribution: Provides empirical updates on student AI perceptions across cohorts and evaluates a multi-dimensional responsible AI integration framework through faculty workshops in a U.S. medical school.
synthesis.limitations: Single institution; incomplete full-text evidence for limitations section; workshop post-sample sizes are small; not focused on conversational system governance mechanisms.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as borderline or contextual supporting evidence for institutional, educational, and policy-oriented responsible AI adoption in regulated healthcare training environments, not as central evidence for conversational LLM governance architectures.

evidence.claim: Peer-reviewed 2026 Cureus journal article on AI in medical curriculum
Study uses generative AI and LLMs in medical education context
evidence.excerpt: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into medical education presents both opportunities and continuing challenges
Large language models (LLMs) have already transformed health professions education.

evidence.claim: Empirical design tracks student attitudes over time
evidence.excerpt: Using our previously published satisfaction instrument, we tracked shifting attitudes toward AI among our pre-clerkship and clerkship students.

evidence.claim: Sample sizes and response rates for rising M3 students
evidence.excerpt: The response rate for AI use was higher in 2026 compared to 2025 (97%, n=68 vs. 89%, n=62) for rising third-year students (class sizes of 80).

evidence.claim: Responsible AI framework and faculty workshops implemented
evidence.excerpt: we developed a multi- dimensional framework for responsible AI integration and implemented a series of faculty development workshops.

evidence.claim: Workshop increased faculty confidence and engagement
evidence.excerpt: The first workshop produced an increase in confidence (+0.75) and practical engagement (+0.43).

evidence.claim: Second workshop emphasized ethics and policy with cautious outlook
evidence.excerpt: A second workshop focused on ethical and policy considerations yielded greater critical awareness, though with a more cautious outlook.

evidence.claim: ChatGPT used in faculty workshop on teaching optimization
evidence.excerpt: The workshop demonstrated how ChatGPT (OpenAI Group PBC, San Francisco, California, United States) could best be used for preparation of teaching materials.

evidence.claim: ChatGPT confidence change was statistically significant
evidence.excerpt: The confidence shift after the workshop (+0.75) is significant (p = 0.013).

evidence.claim: Faculty development needs include prompt engineering and role-specific pathways
evidence.excerpt: Feedback across both workshops consistently highlighted the need for hands- on training, prompt engineering instruction, and role-specific, tool-agnostic development pathways.

evidence.claim: Prior work integrated generative AI while maintaining ethical standards
evidence.excerpt: medical schools can develop and implement plans to integrate generative AI into preclinical curricula while maintaining academic integrity and ethical standards

evidence.claim: No conversational system governance mechanisms described in provided text
